document_check.note: Parra MA, Granada J, Fernandez G. Memory-driven eye movements prospectively predict dementia in people at risk of Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's Dement (DADM) 2022;14:e12386, DOI 10.1002/dad2.12386. The title matches the summaries.md block for Paper 988. The study was run at AXIS Neurociencias, Bahia Blanca, Argentina, with 65 MCI patients and 42 controls. Table 1 (p. 4) gives the MCI-versus-control fixed effects for log fixation duration and saccade amplitude during the visual short-term memory binding (VSTMB) task. This is the study and the result named in cited_result. Registry stub P-1026 is listed as a duplicate of this paper.

cited_result: Group-level MCI (n = 65) versus control (n = 42) differences in eye movements during the VSTMB task, from the first linear model (Group x Condition x Memory Stage; Table 1, p. 4). In MCI, log fixation duration was shorter in every cell (for example, encoding of bound colours: estimate -0.33, t = -42.11) and saccade amplitude was larger (encoding of bound colours: 1.09, t = 18.93), in both the bound-colour (BC) and unbound-colour (UC) conditions and at both encoding and retrieval, against a significance threshold of |t| = 1.95.
tool_reason: The cited result compares eye-movement measures between diagnostic groups at one time point, the baseline assessment. It is not a model's discrimination, a test's accuracy against a reference standard, or the longitudinal conversion result. Following the review's practice (for example P-363 and P-966), the JBI analytical cross-sectional checklist applies, though recruitment by diagnostic group means a case-control reading is also defensible.

domains.domain: Item 1. Criteria for inclusion clearly defined
domains.rationale: For patients, the diagnostic criteria and exclusions are stated: medical causes, vascular lesions on CT or MRI, Axis I disorders, ophthalmological disease and colour blindness, plus a caregiver requirement. For controls, no inclusion criteria are given beyond the ophthalmological exclusions that apply to all participants. The paper does not say how 'healthy' was defined or ascertained.

signalling.question: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
signalling.quote: To be eligible for the study, patients had to have at least one caregiver providing regular care and support.

domains.domain: Item 2. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.rationale: The site (AXIS Neurociencias, Bahia Blanca), the language group, the period (2017 to 2020) and mean age and education per group are reported. Sex distribution, the recruitment source and sampling of either group (consecutive or convenience; where the controls came from), and the numbers screened and excluded are not. I searched Sections 2 and 3 for sex, recruitment route and screening numbers and found none.

signalling.question: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
signalling.quote: The study was carried out at AXIS Neurociencias (Bahía Blanca, Buenos Aires, Argentina) and included native Spanish speakers.

domains.domain: Item 3. Exposure (diagnostic group membership) measured validly and reliably
domains.rationale: Mapping used: exposure = diagnostic group, condition criteria = item 4, outcome = eye-movement measures (item 7). Patients were classified by a psychiatrist and three neurologists after a full clinical work-up. The document does not say how control status was established. The controls' very narrow baseline scores (MMSE 29.7, SD 0.4; ACE-R 93.2, SD 0.8) suggest a highly selected group, and the paper does not explain how it was selected. The two groups were therefore ascertained asymmetrically, as in P-363.

signalling.question: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: Patients were diagnosed based on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition (DSM-IV) criteria and relying on the classical MCI criteria,16,17 which were applied by one psychiatrist and three neurologists.

domains.domain: Item 4. Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition
domains.rationale: Standard frameworks are named (DSM-IV and classical Petersen MCI criteria), but the thresholds for objective impairment are not operationalised. The reported baseline scores sit at the criteria's own limits. The mean Pfeffer functional score of 6.1 is at or above the stated cutoff of 6, which conflicts with the MCI requirement of preserved function. The mean GDS of 8.5 is just under the depression cutoff of 9, although Axis I disorders were an exclusion, and 7 patients later had major depression (p. 7). The authors nonetheless state that the sample met classical criteria. This is scored as P-50 was scored, where the stated criteria conflicted with the reported scores.

signalling.question: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
signalling.quote: The Pfeffer daily activity in MCI was a mean score of 6.1 (SD = 1.5), cutoff of 6, and the Hamilton’s Anxiety Scale in MCI was a mean score of 16.3 (SD = 3.5), with a cutoff of 18.

domains.rationale: Mean age and years of education are reported for each group (73 vs 72 years; 12 vs 12 years). None is named or discussed as a confounder, and they are not tested between groups. Sex is not reported. Mood and anxiety, which were raised in MCI, are not reported for controls and are not considered as influences on oculomotor behaviour. Scored as P-553 and P-661 were: characteristics reported but not identified as confounders.

signalling.question: Were confounding factors identified?
signalling.quote: A total of 65 MCI patients (mean age of 73 SD 6.1 years, mean years of education = 12) and 42 controls (mean age of 72 SD 6.7 years, mean years of education = 12) were enrolled in the study.

domains.domain: Item 6. Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated
domains.rationale: The group model has only Group, Condition and Memory Stage, with no covariates. No matching procedure is described (the paper never calls the controls 'matched'), and nothing is stratified. The only design-level restriction is excluding ophthalmological disease and requiring corrected 20/20 vision. That partly addresses ocular confounders but not sex (unreported), mood, anxiety or medication. The similar mean ages and education years are observed, not designed or tested. Scored as P-966 and P-687 were (unadjusted group comparisons with partial restriction only).

signalling.question: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
signalling.quote: ran our first linear model comprising a between-subjects factor Group (Controls vs MCI patients) and within-subjects factors Condition (UC vs BC) and Memory Stage (Encoding vs Retrieval).

domains.domain: Item 7. Outcomes measured validly and reliably
domains.rationale: Recording conditions were standardised for everyone: a 150 Hz GazePoint tracker with binocular calibration, a chin rest at 60 cm and a fixed monitor. Automated recording limits observer bias. The main text does not report the fixation and saccade detection algorithm or its thresholds, calibration accuracy, data-quality or trial-exclusion rules, or data loss by group. It refers to Supplementary Material, which was not available in the source text. A 150 Hz sampling rate limits precision for saccade amplitude.

signalling.question: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: were recorded with a GazePoint eye tracker, with a sampling rate of 150 Hz. All recordings and calibration were binocular.

domains.rationale: The unit of analysis is not stated, and no subject-level random effect or other allowance for repeated trials and fixations within a person is described. The reported statistics are implausible for a comparison of 107 people, which indicates fixations or trials were treated as independent observations. A 0.33 log-unit group difference has SE 0.00 and t = -42.11, and the behavioural group post hoc test gives t = 112.2 for 63% vs 91% correct. This pseudo-replication inflates significance, as in P-144. Eight group contrasts per measure are judged against an uncorrected |t| = 1.95. The model is unadjusted, and no subject-level group means with dispersion are reported for the eye-movement measures.

signalling.question: Was appropriate statistical analysis used?
signalling.quote: Group differences in the VSTMB task were tested with analysis of variance (ANOVA) and linear regression. [p. 3]; Control vs MCI X BC -0.33 0.00 -42.11 [p. 4]; They revealed that patients in the ADS group performed significantly poorer than Controls on the BC (t = 112.2, p < 0.001) [p. 4]; Threshold of significance is set at t = ±1.95. [p. 4]

applicability.rationale: The sample comes from a single specialist neurocognitive centre in Argentina and is Spanish-speaking only. Ophthalmological disease, vascular lesions and Axis I disorders were excluded, and patients had to have a caregiver. Controls scored near ceiling with very little spread (MMSE SD 0.4), so they may be unusually healthy, which would widen group differences.
Recording used a research set-up (chin rest, fixed monitor, 150 Hz tracker) within a 1.5 h session. The measures come from the developers' commercial VSTMB paradigm (ViewMind).

overall: High risk of bias (JBI analytical cross-sectional checklist; items 6 and 8 are 'No' under the review's rule)
overall_rationale: Two key items are 'No'. The group comparison is unadjusted, with no matching, stratification or covariates (item 6). The analysis appears to treat repeated fixations or trials as independent, which gives implausible t statistics and understated standard errors, with no multiplicity control (item 8). Confounder identification (item 5) and outcome measurement (item 7) are Unclear. Under the review's rule, any 'No' among items 5 to 8 makes the rating high. The direction of the group differences may still be real, since the model estimates are large and consistent across cells, but their stated precision and significance cannot be relied on.
